title: Recursion or a loop?
summary: When recursion is natural, when a loop is better, and how to turn one into the other with your own stack. Delve counts how much of each floor you can reach.

steps.title: Two calls per call
body: Fibonacci numbers: each is the sum of the two before. `0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...`
The definition translates straight into recursion with **two** base cases and **two** recursive calls:
```text
fib(0) = 0      fib(1) = 1      fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
Step through `Fib(4)`. Notice how often `Fib(1)` and `Fib(0)` are computed: the calls branch like a tree, and the same subproblems are solved again and again.

steps.prompt: Count the calls. What is printed?
steps.explain: 15 calls to compute one small number. The count roughly doubles each time `n` goes up by 2: `Fib(40)` needs over 300 million calls.

steps.title: The same thing as a loop
body: A loop can walk *up* from the base cases instead of *down* from `n`, keeping just the last two values in boxes:
```text
repeat n times:  a, b = b, a + b
answer is a
Each pass is a small **swap-and-add**, exactly like the swap from module 1. It does `n` steps instead of exponentially many.

steps.prompt: Arrange the loop body so the program prints `8` (the 6th Fibonacci number, counting from 0).
steps.explain: Compute the new value before you overwrite anything, just like saving into `temp` before a swap.

steps.prompt: Which tool is the more natural fit?
items: Visiting every folder inside a folder, at any depth
Exploring every path through a maze
Reading lines until the input ends
steps.explain: Recursion shines when the data is itself nested (folders in folders, branches of a tree). For a straight line of items, a loop is simpler and uses no extra stack.

steps.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Any loop can be rewritten as recursion, and vice versa
Deep recursion can run out of stack space where a loop would not
Recursion is always faster than a loop
Naive recursive Fibonacci repeats the same work many times
steps.explain: They are equally powerful, but each recursive call costs a stack frame, and naive branching recursion can repeat work exponentially.

steps.title: Fast Fibonacci
prompt: Write `long Fib(int n)` using a **loop**, so `Fib(80)` returns instantly. `Fib(0)` is 0, `Fib(1)` is 1, `Fib(10)` is 55.
Use `long`: `Fib(80)` is far too big for an `int`.
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("Fib(0)", 0L, Fib(0));
Dojo.Eq("Fib(1)", 1L, Fib(1));
Dojo.Eq("Fib(10)", 55L, Fib(10));
hints: Two boxes `a = 0`, `b = 1`. Repeat `n` times: compute `a + b`, then shift both along.

steps.title: Sum an array recursively
prompt: Write `int SumFrom(int[] a, int i)` that returns the sum of `a[i]`, `a[i+1]`, ... to the end, **recursively** with no loops. `SumFrom(a, 0)` is the whole sum.
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("SumFrom({ 4, 5, 6 }, 0)", 15, SumFrom(new[] { 4, 5, 6 }, 0));
Dojo.Eq("SumFrom({ 4, 5, 6 }, 2)", 6, SumFrom(new[] { 4, 5, 6 }, 2));
Dojo.Eq("SumFrom({ 4, 5, 6 }, 3) is empty", 0, SumFrom(new[] { 4, 5, 6 }, 3));
Dojo.Eq("SumFrom({ }, 0)", 0, SumFrom(new int[0], 0));
hints: Base case: when `i` reaches the end there is nothing left to add.

steps.title: Flood fill, and running out of stack
body: To count the tiles reachable from a start, **flood fill**: visit a tile, mark it, then visit its four neighbours that are not walls and not yet marked. Recursively that is a few lines:
```csharp
int Fill(string[] map, bool[,] done, int x, int y)
if (IsWall(map, x, y) || done[y, x]) return 0;
done[y, x] = true;
return 1 + Fill(map, done, x + 1, y) + Fill(map, done, x - 1, y)
+ Fill(map, done, x, y + 1) + Fill(map, done, x, y - 1);

But every call is a frame on the call stack, and a long corridor of 100,000 tiles is 100,000 frames deep: a `StackOverflowException`, which ends the program and cannot be caught. The fix is to keep the list of "tiles still to visit" yourself, in a `Stack<int>`, and loop until it is empty. The work is identical; only the bookkeeping moved from the call stack to your stack.
One number per tile is enough: `y * width + x` packs a position, and `pos % width`, `pos / width` unpack it (module 1 says hello).

steps.title: How much of the floor can you reach?
prompt: Write **`static int CountReachable(string[] map, int startX, int startY)`**: how many tiles that are not walls can be reached from the start by steps north, south, east and west. Delve prints it when you enter a floor and turns it into "Explored 43%".
Do it **with a loop and your own `Stack<int>`**, not recursion: Delve's maps are small, but this function must work on any map.
- Keep a `bool[,] done` grid (`new bool[map.Length, width]`) so no tile is counted twice.
- Use your **`IsWall(map, x, y)`** from Logic (the checks supply the reference version): it already treats off-the-map as a wall.
The start tile is never a wall. On `{ "#####", "#..##", "##.##", "#####" }` from (1, 1) the answer is 3.
starter: static int CountReachable(string[] map, int startX, int startY)
solution: static int CountReachable(string[] map, int startX, int startY)
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Try("CountReachable never crashes", () =>
Dojo.Eq("three tiles in an L", 3, CountReachable(new[] { "#####", "#..##", "##.##", "#####" }, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("a closed room counts only itself", 1, CountReachable(new[] { "###", "#.#", "###" }, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("a separate cave is not reachable", 2, CountReachable(new[] { "#######", "#..#..#", "#######" }, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("items and monsters are not walls", 5, CountReachable(new[] { "#######", "#.g$>k#", "#######" }, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("a loop is counted once", 8, CountReachable(new[] { "#####", "#...#", "#.#.#", "#...#", "#####" }, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("an open map with no outer wall", 6, CountReachable(new[] { "...", "..." }, 0, 0));
var dojoBig = new string[300];
for (int r = 0; r < 300; r++) dojoBig[r] = new string('.', 300);
Dojo.Eq("a huge open cave (90,000 tiles)", 90000, CountReachable(dojoBig, 0, 0));
// src/Bounds.cs, as the reference solution wrote it
static bool IsOutsideMap(int x, int y, int width, int height)
return x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= width || y >= height;
static bool IsWall(string[] map, int x, int y)
return IsOutsideMap(x, y, map[0].Length, map.Length) || map[y][x] == '#';

forbid.message: Uses a loop and a stack, not recursion
Every function starts with `static` (Delve keeps its pieces in one static class)

hints: Loop `while (todo.Count > 0)`: pop a position, unpack `x = pos % width`, `y = pos / width`. If it is already done, `continue`; otherwise mark it and count it.
Then for each of the four neighbours that is not a wall and not done, push `ny * width + nx`.
IsWall comes before `done[ny, nx]` in the condition: off the map, `done` has no box to read.

build.title: Reachable tiles
build.unlocks: Delve knows how big each floor is, and shows how much of it you explored.
